json.title: Stardew Valley
json.genre: Farming and life-management simulation with role-playing elements
json.target_player: Players who enjoy relaxed planning, customization, relationships, collecting, and gradual growth
json.goal: Build a thriving farm and satisfying town life by choosing personal goals such as earning money, restoring the Community Center, developing relationships, exploring, and completing collections.
json.core_action: Repeatedly inspect the farm and town, choose how to spend the day, perform short actions such as planting, watering, harvesting, fishing, mining, crafting, shopping, and talking, then convert the results into money, materials, relationships, or progress.
json.information: The player observes the time, date, season, weather forecast, energy and health, crop growth, available money and materials, tool capabilities, shop offerings, requests, relationship levels, map locations, and predictable schedules or preferences learned over time.
constraints: Each day has limited time.
Most physical actions consume energy.
Crops grow only in appropriate seasons unless protected by special facilities.
Money, seeds, materials, inventory space, and tool quality limit available plans.
Characters, shops, fish, festivals, and resources may be available only at particular times, locations, seasons, or weather conditions.
Travel between activities consumes part of the day.
decisions: Which activities deserve today's limited time and energy
Whether to invest money in seeds, animals, tools, buildings, inventory, or other upgrades
Which crops to grow and whether to sell, process, store, gift, cook, or donate the output
Whether to pursue income, relationships, exploration, collections, or long-term restoration goals
How much risk and inventory space to commit to a mining trip
How to arrange and automate the farm
json.feedback: Actions produce immediate sounds, animations, item drops, energy changes, dialogue reactions, and visible task completion. Crops and buildings visibly develop over days, sales are summarized overnight, relationships gain hearts, skills level up, and collections or restoration projects fill in.
json.failure: There is usually no permanent game-over state. Running out of health or staying out too late can end the day and may cost money or items; neglected seasonal crops can die, and poor planning can waste time, energy, or investment. Most losses can be recovered through additional days of play.
json.retry_motivation: A failed or inefficient day reveals schedules, resource requirements, and better routines. Persistent farm growth, unfinished projects, upcoming seasons, character stories, and the possibility of a more efficient plan encourage another day.
json.mastery: Skilled players coordinate seasonal calendars, processing chains, character schedules, weather, travel routes, tool upgrades, and energy restoration. They turn early investments into automation and high-value production while pursuing several goals in the same trip.
json.variation: Seasons, weather, daily luck, resource drops, mine layouts, requests, festivals, chosen farm layout, crop strategy, relationships, specialization choices, and self-selected goals change the experience.
json.progression: New seasons introduce different crops, fish, events, and planning problems. Skill levels, tool upgrades, buildings, crafting recipes, relationships, deeper mine floors, restored locations, and story milestones gradually expand the player's options and production scale.
json.reward: Money, harvests, new items, upgraded tools, recipes, buildings, automated systems, relationship scenes, collection completion, restored spaces, visual farm improvement, and the satisfaction of executing a planned day reinforce the loop.
json.core_loop_statement: Read the day's conditions, choose a small set of priorities, perform work, and convert the results into future capability before time and energy run out. The thinking lives in balancing attractive short-term activities against investments that make later days easier or more valuable.
json.mastery_statement: A novice reacts to nearby tasks and frequently runs out of time or energy. An expert plans around calendars and routes, bundles compatible errands together, and builds systems that reduce repetitive work.
json.replay_statement: Next time, the player can choose a different farm layout, income strategy, relationship focus, upgrade order, or daily route. Even within one save, every new day supports a revised plan based on what the previous day taught.
json.kid_translation_note: A career game could give children a short workday, several useful tasks, and a visible workplace that improves through their choices. Simple calendars and limited energy can teach prioritization without making mistakes permanently punishing.

json.title: Pokémon Red/Blue
json.genre: Creature-collection role-playing game with turn-based battles
json.target_player: Children and general audiences who enjoy collecting, exploration, tactical battles, discovery, and creature growth
json.goal: Explore the region, catch and train a varied team, earn eight Gym Badges, defeat the Pokémon League, and optionally complete the Pokédex.
json.core_action: Explore routes and dungeons, encounter creatures or trainers, read battle conditions, choose a move, item, switch, or escape, then use the outcome to strengthen or revise the team.
json.information: The player reads creature species, level, current HP, status conditions, known moves, move type, remaining PP, opponent identity, battle messages, inventory, party order, terrain obstacles, NPC hints, and knowledge accumulated about type matchups and encounter locations.
constraints: The active party holds at most six Pokémon.
Each Pokémon can know at most four moves.
Moves have limited PP between restorations.
HP and status persist between many battles until healed.
Catching requires Poké Balls and is easier after weakening or inflicting status on the target.
Badge and field-move requirements gate parts of the world.
Items and money are limited, especially early in the journey.
Some Pokémon are exclusive to one version or normally require trading to obtain.
decisions: Which species and roles to include in the six-member party
Whether to attack, use a status or setup move, switch, use an item, or attempt escape
Which four moves each Pokémon should retain
Whether to catch, train, evolve, store, or replace a creature
How to balance team training instead of relying on one highly leveled creature
When to spend consumable items or return to a healing location
Which routes and optional areas to explore
json.feedback: Battles show HP changes, animations, sound effects, effectiveness messages, status effects, experience gains, level-ups, stat increases, evolution, and victory rewards. The Pokédex records discoveries, badges mark major progress, and newly learned field abilities open previously blocked paths.
json.failure: If every party member faints, the player blacks out, loses a portion of carried money, and returns to the most recent healing location. Battle and travel progress since the last save can also be lost if the player reloads, but trained creatures and collected resources otherwise persist after a blackout.
json.retry_motivation: The player can train, change the party, revise moves, buy supplies, study type matchups, or approach with a different lead. Near victories clearly suggest that one more level or a better tactical choice could succeed.
json.mastery: Skilled players anticipate opposing types and moves, preserve favorable matchups through switching, use status and stat-changing moves deliberately, manage PP and items across long routes, and construct a team with complementary strengths rather than selecting only by level.
json.variation: Wild encounters, capture success, critical hits, damage ranges, status effects, move accuracy, chosen starter, team composition, learned moves, evolution timing, route order, and version-exclusive species create different journeys.
json.progression: Routes introduce stronger and more varied opponents, while badges, field moves, and key items unlock new areas. Captures, experience, levels, evolutions, and new moves steadily increase team capability before the final sequence of elite battles.
json.reward: New creatures, Pokédex entries, experience, levels, moves, evolutions, money, items, badges, opened routes, memorable team attachment, and victories produced by a well-built team reinforce play.
json.core_loop_statement: Explore, encounter a challenge, choose actions from a compact battle menu, and turn victories or captures into a stronger and more flexible team. The thinking lives in matching capabilities to opponents while deciding which creatures deserve limited team space and training.
json.mastery_statement: A novice mainly uses the strongest-looking attack and favors the highest-level creature. An expert predicts matchups, switches proactively, values support moves, and develops a balanced team whose members cover one another's weaknesses.
json.replay_statement: A new journey can use a different starter, party, move set, evolution plan, or training balance. Individual defeats also invite an immediate experiment with another lead, matchup, or item strategy.
json.kid_translation_note: Career roles could become a small team of workers with different strengths, letting children match the right skill to each job. Growth should make familiar teammates visibly more capable while encouraging a balanced team rather than one universally best choice.

json.title: Zoombinis
json.target_player: Children developing logical reasoning, pattern recognition, hypothesis testing, and problem-solving skills
json.goal: Guide groups of Zoombinis through a sequence of logic puzzles to reach the safe settlement of Zoombiniville.
json.core_action: Observe a puzzle's reactions, compare Zoombini attributes, infer the hidden rule, then place or route each character according to the current hypothesis.
json.information: The player observes combinations of visible attributes such as hair, eyes, noses, and feet; puzzle layouts; environmental clues; accepted and rejected attempts; limited attempt indicators; and patterns connecting a character's features to successful destinations or arrangements.
constraints: Each traveling group contains a limited number of individually featured Zoombinis.
Puzzle rules must often be inferred from examples rather than stated directly.
Many puzzles allow only a limited number of incorrect attempts.
A wrong assignment may prevent one or more Zoombinis from continuing through that puzzle.
Later difficulty levels use more attributes, categories, exceptions, or interacting rules.
The player may need to continue with a smaller group after mistakes.
decisions: Which Zoombini to test first to gain the most useful information
Which visible attributes are relevant to the hidden rule
How to classify, order, pair, or route the group
Whether the evidence supports the current hypothesis
When to use a remaining mistake allowance on an uncertain test
How to revise the rule after a rejection
json.feedback: Puzzle characters and machines visibly accept or reject choices through expressive animations, sounds, and reactions. Successful Zoombinis move onward, mistakes consume opportunities or leave travelers behind, and arrival at camps or Zoombiniville makes rescued population progress visible.
json.failure: Incorrect choices can exhaust a puzzle's allowed mistakes and cause affected Zoombinis to be turned back or left unable to continue with the current group. The broader rescue campaign continues, so the player can bring later groups and use improved reasoning rather than facing a conventional game over.
json.retry_motivation: Every rejection is evidence about the hidden rule, making the next attempt better informed. Attachment to the distinctive characters, the desire to bring everyone safely home, and access to another group encourage renewed attempts.
json.mastery: Skilled players choose highly informative tests, isolate one variable at a time, track both positive and negative evidence, and infer general rules before committing the whole group. They minimize guesses and can explain why each placement should work.
json.variation: Zoombini feature combinations, group composition, puzzle instances, hidden mappings, chosen journey routes, surviving group size, and escalating puzzle difficulty vary the reasoning problem.
json.progression: The journey chains different kinds of logic problems together, and repeated journeys raise puzzle difficulty. Advanced versions demand classification across more features, multi-step deduction, tighter error management, and more complex relationships.
json.reward: Safe passage, expressive character celebrations, a growing Zoombiniville population, access to later journey sections, successful rule discovery, and the intrinsic satisfaction of a complete logical explanation reinforce play.
json.core_loop_statement: Observe attributes, test a classification or route, interpret acceptance or rejection, and refine the hidden rule until the group passes. The fun lives in converting playful reactions into evidence and reaching certainty with as few risky guesses as possible.
json.mastery_statement: A novice guesses from superficial resemblance and changes theories inconsistently. An expert designs informative tests, controls variables, remembers rejected cases, and applies a discovered rule to the entire group.
json.replay_statement: The next group presents different feature combinations and may expose weaknesses in the player's previous rule-finding method. A player can retry by testing a more diagnostic character first or by tracking evidence more systematically.
json.kid_translation_note: A career game could ask children to assign customers, tools, or materials by discovering a workplace rule from reactions. Friendly feedback can make mistakes useful clues, teaching that careful observation is part of real work.

json.title: Cooking Mama
json.genre: Cooking-themed collection of timing, motion, and dexterity minigames
json.target_player: Children, families, and casual players who enjoy short tactile challenges, recognizable food preparation, and score improvement
json.goal: Complete recipes by succeeding at a sequence of preparation and cooking minigames, earning strong evaluations and unlocking or completing more dishes.
json.core_action: Read a brief visual instruction, then repeatedly perform a short timed input such as chopping, stirring, peeling, pouring, shaping, controlling heat, or flipping food with the required rhythm and precision.
json.information: The player observes gesture demonstrations, tool and ingredient positions, timers, progress indicators, target shapes or quantities, color and cooking-state changes, warning cues, and Mama's immediate reactions.
constraints: Most recipe steps have strict time limits.
Inputs must follow the demonstrated direction, rhythm, order, or target area.
Overcooking, undercooking, spilling, inaccurate cutting, or missed timing lowers performance.
A recipe combines several different minigames, so one weak step can reduce the final evaluation.
The control scheme limits each task to a small set of gestures or button actions.
decisions: How quickly to work without losing accuracy
When to stop heating, pouring, stirring, or cutting
How to adjust motion after visual or audio warnings
Whether to prioritize clean precision or rapid completion when time is short
Which recipe to practice or attempt next
json.feedback: Ingredients visibly transform and tools respond directly to input. Timers, progress meters, success effects, mistakes, Mama's expressions and comments, per-step results, and a final recipe evaluation show performance.
json.failure: A poorly performed step produces a low evaluation or an imperfect dish rather than usually ending the entire game. The player generally continues to later steps and can replay the recipe to improve the result.
json.retry_motivation: Challenges are brief, mistakes are easy to identify, and better timing can quickly produce a higher rating. The humor of imperfect outcomes, Mama's reactions, recipe completion, and the desire to master every step support replay.
json.mastery: Skilled players recognize each minigame's cue-to-action pattern, use controlled and efficient motions, anticipate state changes instead of reacting late, and maintain accuracy under the timer across the full recipe.
json.variation: Recipes use different ingredient transformations, tools, gestures, timing windows, action sequences, and combinations of minigames. Performance variation also comes from the player's speed and precision.
json.progression: New recipes introduce different actions and more demanding combinations of familiar gestures. Improvement comes both from accessing more content and from learning the timing and control language shared by multiple recipe steps.
json.reward: Completed dishes, scores or evaluations, positive character reactions, unlocked recipes or content, visual food transformations, and immediate improvement over a previous attempt reinforce the loop.
json.core_loop_statement: Watch a tiny demonstration, perform one tactile job under time pressure, receive an immediate evaluation, and continue to the next step until the product is complete. The fun lives in turning recognizable work motions into short precision challenges and seeing raw ingredients transform.
json.mastery_statement: A novice reacts late, moves too broadly, or rushes and makes messy inputs. An expert anticipates cues, uses compact controlled motions, and balances speed with accuracy across every step.
json.replay_statement: The player can repeat a recipe to improve the weakest step, achieve a better final rating, or practice a troublesome gesture. Different recipes recombine familiar skills in new sequences.
json.kid_translation_note: A career activity could divide a real job into three or four safe, exaggerated gestures with clear demonstrations and visible results. Each step should be brief and forgiving while still rewarding careful timing.

json.title: The Oregon Trail
json.genre: Educational journey, resource-management, and risk simulation
json.target_player: Students and general players interested in historical journeys, planning, survival decisions, and emergent stories
json.goal: Lead a traveling party from Missouri to Oregon while managing supplies, health, time, weather, terrain, and unpredictable hazards.
json.core_action: Review party and resource status, choose purchases, pace, rations, routes, rests, river-crossing methods, and responses to events, then advance the journey and absorb the resulting costs or benefits.
json.information: The player reads distance, date, weather, terrain, party health, illnesses or injuries, food, ammunition, clothing, spare parts, money, wagon condition, landmark information, river depth and width, event messages, and advice available at stops.
constraints: Money at departure limits the initial supply mix.
Food, ammunition, clothing, medicine-related capacity, and wagon parts are finite.
Travel consumes food and calendar time.
Faster pace and lower rations can increase health risk.
Weather and seasons can make late arrival dangerous.
Wagon breakdowns require appropriate spare parts or costly delay.
River crossings force choices under incomplete risk information.
Random illness, injury, theft, loss, and death can undermine a sound plan.
decisions: How to allocate starting money across supplies
Which departure month balances preparation and seasonal risk
How fast to travel and how much food to ration
When to rest, trade, buy supplies, hunt, or continue
Which river-crossing method is worth its cost and risk
Whether a shortcut saves enough time to justify uncertainty
How to respond when several scarce resources are low at once
json.feedback: Status screens and event text report changing health, supplies, distance, date, breakdowns, illnesses, deaths, and environmental conditions. The wagon advances across a map, landmarks confirm progress, and the ending evaluates survival and remaining resources.
json.failure: Party members can die from illness, injury, starvation, exposure, accidents, or other hazards. The expedition can end when the entire party dies or can no longer continue; even a successful arrival may receive a weaker result if few people or supplies survive.
json.retry_motivation: A failed expedition creates a memorable causal story: too little food, a late departure, excessive pace, a dangerous crossing, or simple bad luck. Players retry to test a different supply plan, risk policy, route, or pacing strategy and see whether they can bring more people through.
json.mastery: Skilled players maintain reserves, understand the interaction between season, pace, rations, and health, avoid spending scarce resources on low-value choices, and select risks based on current recovery capacity rather than treating every event independently.
json.variation: Random weather, illness, accidents, river conditions, losses, hunting results, party composition, chosen occupation, starting purchases, routes, pace, and player risk tolerance create different expedition stories.
json.progression: The journey moves through landmarks and increasingly consequential resource pressure. Supplies decline, winter approaches, terrain changes, and accumulated injuries or equipment losses make later decisions depend on the quality of earlier planning.
json.reward: Distance traveled, landmark arrival, surviving party members, preserved supplies, successful risk management, final score, historical context, and the emergent story of the expedition reinforce play.
json.core_loop_statement: Inspect the expedition's condition, choose how much resource or risk to accept, advance toward the next landmark, and update the plan after events occur. The thinking lives in preserving enough flexibility for unknown future trouble while a seasonal deadline keeps the party moving.
json.mastery_statement: A novice optimizes the immediate problem or spends resources until a meter looks safe. An expert manages interacting reserves, thinks several landmarks ahead, and judges each risk by whether the party could recover from a bad outcome.
json.replay_statement: Another expedition can change the departure date, occupation, shopping list, pace, rationing, route, and crossing policy. Because events vary, the player can compare whether a strategy was robust or merely lucky.
json.kid_translation_note: A career journey could ask children to prepare a limited tool kit and guide a team through a workday containing uncertain requests. Keep consequences nonfatal and frame reserves, rest, and asking for help as responsible professional choices.

json.title: Two Point Hospital
json.target_player: Players who enjoy systems management, spatial planning, optimization, workplace simulation, and humorous problem-solving
json.goal: Design and operate hospitals that diagnose and cure patients while maintaining finances, staff performance, reputation, and scenario-specific objectives.
json.core_action: Observe patient flow and hospital statistics, build or modify rooms, hire and assign staff, adjust priorities and policies, then watch the simulation reveal queues, bottlenecks, costs, and treatment outcomes.
json.information: The player observes patient needs and paths, diagnosis progress, queues, room utilization, staff skills and traits, energy and morale, salary expectations, machine condition, cleanliness, temperature, attractiveness, finances, cure rate, reputation, emergencies, inspections, and scenario objectives.
constraints: Construction, equipment, salaries, training, and maintenance cost money.
Rooms require minimum sizes, doors, and particular equipment.
Only qualified staff can perform many specialized jobs.
Patients must move through diagnosis before appropriate treatment.
Walking distance and queues reduce throughput and patient survival chances.
Staff require breaks and can become tired, unhappy, or overworked.
Machines deteriorate and may require maintenance.
Building space and available plots limit layout.
Scenario star objectives require several performance targets at once.
decisions: Which rooms to build, where to place them, and when to duplicate them
Which applicants to hire and which skills to train
How to assign staff roles and break policies
Whether to prioritize diagnosis certainty, treatment speed, patient survival, or financial efficiency
When to expand into another building
How much to invest in room quality, machines, amenities, janitors, and support infrastructure
How to redesign the hospital when queues expose a bottleneck
json.feedback: Patients and staff visibly navigate the hospital, queues form outside rooms, machines operate or break, and humorous cures animate successful treatment. Pop-up messages, financial graphs, queue counts, cure rates, deaths, reputation, awards, inspections, emergencies, and objective meters quantify results.
json.failure: Poor management can cause long queues, low cure rates, deaths, unhappy staff, damaged reputation, and sustained financial losses. A hospital may become financially unsustainable, while individual scenario objectives can remain unmet until the player redesigns or improves operations.
json.retry_motivation: Bottlenecks are visible and invite targeted fixes such as another room, better routing, specialized training, or changed priorities. New layouts and staffing models can produce dramatic improvements, and higher scenario ratings reward continued optimization.
json.mastery: Skilled players design short patient routes, separate high-volume functions from specialist treatment, train focused staff, use job assignments deliberately, maintain spare capacity, and diagnose the actual system bottleneck before spending money.
json.variation: Patient arrivals, disease mix, staff applicant traits, emergencies, inspections, epidemics, maps, building shapes, climate conditions, objectives, layout choices, and staffing strategies vary hospital operation.
json.progression: Scenarios introduce new illnesses, diagnostic and treatment rooms, staff skills, environmental problems, and management objectives. One-, two-, and three-star targets demand increasingly strong performance, while unlocked tools support more complex hospitals.
json.reward: Treatment income, cure animations, expanding buildings, trained staff, improved statistics, higher reputation, awards, scenario stars, unlocked equipment and locations, and smoothly flowing patient traffic reinforce the loop.
json.core_loop_statement: Build a service system, watch workers and customers move through it, identify the next bottleneck, and spend limited resources to improve flow. The fun lives in discovering that layout, training, maintenance, and staffing interact, then seeing a redesigned workplace run smoothly.
json.mastery_statement: A novice reacts to the loudest queue by adding expensive rooms. An expert traces the whole service chain, distinguishes symptoms from root bottlenecks, specializes staff, and designs capacity and walking routes before demand peaks.
json.replay_statement: The same workplace problem can be addressed through a compact layout, extra capacity, better-trained staff, different diagnostic policies, or slower expansion. New maps and disease mixes test whether the player's management principles generalize.
json.kid_translation_note: A simplified career game could show customers moving through three workplace stations and let children place workers according to their skills. Visible queues make the effect of cooperation, layout, training, and rest understandable without exposing children to complex financial controls.

json.title: PowerWash Simulator
json.genre: First-person methodical cleaning and work simulation
json.target_player: Players who enjoy low-pressure tasks, visible completion, precise tool use, exploration of detailed objects, and relaxing audiovisual feedback
json.goal: Remove dirt from every required surface of each job site until the cleaning checklist reaches full completion.
json.core_action: Scan an object for remaining dirt, choose a washer configuration, aim and sweep the water stream across surfaces, reposition to reach hidden areas, and repeat until each component is marked clean.
json.information: The player observes dirty and clean surface contrast, a dirt-highlighting function, overall and component completion percentages, a list of object parts, cleaning completion notifications, surface distance and angle, washer strength, nozzle width, and the geometry of inaccessible areas.
constraints: Different washers and nozzles trade cleaning power for spray width or effective range.
Dirt may be hidden beneath, behind, above, or inside complex objects.
The water stream requires line of sight and an effective angle and distance.
Ladders, scaffolding, crouching, and repositioning are needed to reach some surfaces.
A component is not complete until nearly all of its required dirty area is removed.
Large jobs require sustained attention across many separately tracked parts.
decisions: Which section to clean first
Whether to use a narrow powerful stream or a wider faster sweep
Where to stand to expose the most surface area
When to clean methodically versus search specifically for missed spots
How to divide a large object into manageable zones
Whether a stubborn mark reflects insufficient power, poor angle, distance, or an overlooked surface
json.feedback: Dirt disappears exactly where the stream passes, revealing brighter colors and materials. Water sounds and visual spray accompany the action, component percentages rise, a distinctive notification marks each fully cleaned part, the checklist shrinks, payment is awarded, and a completion time-lapse summarizes the transformation.
json.failure: Standard jobs generally have little punitive failure. Inefficient technique mainly costs time and attention; the common obstacle is reaching a very high completion percentage while a tiny hidden patch remains. Progress is persistent enough that the player can continue searching rather than restart the job.
json.retry_motivation: The player is usually motivated to continue rather than retry because every cleaned patch remains as visible progress. Missed dirt becomes a contained search problem, while new jobs offer fresh shapes, transformations, tools, and opportunities for a more orderly technique.
json.mastery: Skilled players segment objects into zones, maintain consistent sweep spacing, select nozzles by dirt and geometry, work from angles that expose multiple surfaces, use the dirt highlight diagnostically, and consult component completion data to narrow the final search.
json.variation: Job size, object geometry, dirt coverage, surface materials, access angles, available equipment, optional cleaning order, and the player's chosen workflow vary the experience.
json.progression: Jobs grow from smaller objects to large, intricate environments containing many components and hidden surfaces. Earnings and career progress provide access to stronger washers, attachments, and equipment that improve reach or efficiency.
json.reward: Immediate clean streaks, revealed colors, component-completion notifications, rising percentages, money, equipment upgrades, finished-job transformations, checklist completion, and the final time-lapse reinforce the loop.
json.core_loop_statement: Choose a surface, sweep away visible dirt, inspect the result, and reposition or change tools for whatever remains. The pleasure comes from continuous before-and-after feedback, while the thinking lies in coverage patterns, tool choice, and locating the final hidden patches.
json.mastery_statement: A novice sprays wherever dirt is obvious and later searches a chaotic collection of missed spots. An expert cleans in deliberate zones, controls overlap and angle, and uses part-level information to finish with minimal backtracking.
json.replay_statement: A later job can be approached with a different cleaning order, nozzle strategy, route, or division into zones. Players can also try to produce a cleaner workflow with fewer missed patches and less repositioning.
json.kid_translation_note: A children's career game could turn tidying, inspecting, repairing, painting, or sorting into a persistent visible transformation with a checklist of small parts. A highlight button for remaining work preserves satisfaction while preventing the final search from becoming frustrating.
